note: The registries the governance clauses read. This file is DATA — it changes when packages, surfaces or owners change. The clauses that read it are CODE (tools/governance/src/lib/governance-model.ts) — they change only by founder ruling on architecture. Nothing here is a per-pair verdict; verdicts are derived.

roles.note: A package's role comes from the `workspaces` glob in the root manifest that claims it — never from matching its directory path (Ruling 5). Adding a role folder is an edit here plus an edit to `workspaces`, and nothing else.

containment.note: A service lives inside exactly one layer. A layer belongs to itself. Composition roots live outside the tree and are the only actors permitted to reach across it.

surfaces.note: Who may name this surface. `everyone` = any actor; `composition roots` = the roles above plus the repo root; a list = exactly those roles or package names; an empty list = nobody.

framework/domain-model.why: the product's nouns — the closed sets, the wire shapes and the pure predicates over them. Nothing here declares a port and nothing here carries a dependency a browser cannot run. The one successor of the old substrate that keeps universal reach, for the same reason db:row-type has it: a shape is not an access path.

framework/diagnostics.why: the structured logger, the secret scrubber, and the observability event/adapter contract with its console sink. A log line happens where the process is and every service runs in one; every application installs a sink. `layer` is deliberately not granted, because core-ui is a layer and must not log — core-api and agent-orchestration are named individually instead, the same reason `run-orchestration-composition.ts` (AU31 §2.1(b), relocated into agent-orchestration's own boot) logs a summarized tool arg.

framework/harness-capability.why: what an installed harness IS — its readiness, the models it offers, the tools it already has, the auth action it needs, and how its return enforcement is provisioned. A screen renders this; run-orchestration provisions the enforcement channel; agent-execution's own boot (AU31 §6) types the `ReturnEnforcementChannel` its `returnStatusTool` adapter carries out to the layer that consumes it. Separating it from the protocol is what lets the protocol say no to the interface.

framework/work-intent-port.why: the recorder/reader seam a core-api route uses to write an agent work intent into a table agent-orchestration owns. A port exists to keep two named layers from naming each other, so its audience is the writing side and the owning side, and nobody else.

framework/event-bus.why: the in-process publish/subscribe object. Every server layer publishes on it, any service may publish, and an application composes it at boot — so those are granted by role. A browser has no in-process bus; it has HTTP and SSE, and it reaches the event types in framework/domain-model.

framework/presentation-format.why: a value turned into the string a human reads. Outside the framework role, two packages format anything: the interface, and the one layer that composes a user-visible string on the server. The design system formats too, and reaches this as one framework package naming another. A future service formatting something is a prediction, not a rule about the role.

framework/block-derivation.why: markdown text turned into the block tree the renderer walks, and the content-addressed id that keeps a block stable across edits. Deriving blocks means running a markdown parser and a hash; the interface is the only package outside the framework role that renders block content, and this is the only manifest that carries the parser. The design system renders it too and reaches this as one framework package naming another.

framework/conversation-parts.why: the Part vocabulary and the adapters that derive Parts from messages and session activity. There is exactly one conversation surface. A second consumer of the Part vocabulary means a second conversation, which is a product decision, not an import.

framework/factory-defaults.why: the roster and the system-prompt templates a fresh installation is seeded with. It reads template files off disk, so a browser cannot run it at all.

framework/http-middleware.why: the primitives a route file on either application's Hono app needs. Only the two layers that publish an HTTP API and the two services that mount a route or compare a key. This is the package that carries hono, and the reason thirty other manifests stop carrying it. `composeApiApplication` (AU31 §5.3, relocated here from the deleted `@hyperidle/shared`) is the layer-blind Hono mount recipe both Applications build their one composed app from — `remote-server` and `desktop` name it directly rather than each other, closing the `application → application` crossing AU31 found.

framework/harness-protocol.why: how a run is dispatched to a harness and how its output comes back: the adapter interface, the event stream, the worker wire protocol, the return-action set, and the tool-seam contract (RegisteredTool, ToolResult, ok/err) the tool dispatch side agrees on. A contract between a harness process, the layer that runs it and the worker that hosts it. The web UI is not one of those. `agent-execution`'s own boot (AU31 §6, `bootAgentExecution`) is the layer that runs it — it types the enforcement registry, the harness adapter and the worker-registration message its `AgentExecutionAdapters` bundle carries out to whichever layer consumes it; neither server Application needs the protocol itself, only the already-typed function value the boot hands back. `tool-handlers`, `review`, and `settings` reach it because AU44 batch 5 dissolved `framework/tool-protocol` into this package — those three services formerly reached `tool-protocol` for the RegisteredTool/ToolResult seam, widening harness-protocol's declared audience beyond the harness contract itself.

framework/db.why: the manifest-level dependency on the database package. Which surface INSIDE it you may touch is decided per surface below, so declaring the dependency is not itself a decision.

framework/api-contract.why: the request/response shapes two layers agree on. A service talks through its own layer, so it has no business naming the contract directly.

framework/design-system.why: there is exactly one user interface. A second consumer of the design system means a second interface, which is a product decision, not an import.

db:client.why: holding a database handle is not the same as touching a table

db:row-type.why: a row type is a shape, not an access path

db:schema-ns.why: one import that hands over every table at once. The database's own client factory does the same job for the one legitimate use.

db:unknown.why: an export of the database package that belongs to no named surface. Reaching it means the surface has not been decided yet.

db:testing.why: development code. A production file naming it is already an error under the production-may-not-name-development clause; this entry keeps the two answers from disagreeing.

core-api/credentials.why: The credential store and its AES-256-GCM cipher (moved from @hyperidle/credential-access). core-api consumes the store directly; both server Applications compose the cipher at boot to inject into agent-orchestration via bootAgentOrchestration.

databasePackage.note: `framework/db` is not one target — it is several surfaces with different rules (Ruling 11.2). Which surface an import lands on is decided by the MODULE the symbol is defined in. Tables and row types are detected from the schema source itself, so they are absent here. A module not listed falls to `db:unknown` and is reported — guessing its surface would be fabrication.

endpoints.note: A door is dialled only if the target declares it.

httpApiLayers.why: a layer that publishes an HTTP API publishes it to the whole system. agent-execution is absent because it hosts no API.

mcpRouter.why: the router exists to serve the harness. Only the layer that owns the harness relationship, and the harness itself, dial it.

eventBus.typesNote: Every event the bus can carry, declared as `readonly type: "..."`. An emit or subscribe naming something absent from this module is not a bus event — filtering on it is what keeps ordinary `.on()` and `.emit()` calls from being counted as crossings.
eventBus.why: the framework provides the bus. A framework package that also publishes on it is both the pipe and the water, and the bus can no longer be reasoned about from the outside.

rawRuntime.why: every model and agent call goes through one door so it can be recorded, priced and replayed. Importing a vendor SDK or spawning an agent CLI anywhere else builds a path the rest of the system cannot see.
rawRuntime.spellingNote: Ruling 14 — importing the SDK and spawning the CLI are ONE act with two spellings, and one target. They used to be two targets, which let the development world hold the import and wave the spawn through the same door.

oneDoorSurfaces.note: The development world relaxes every production rule EXCEPT these. Each names a surface where production has exactly one door — going around it builds a world production cannot produce, which is the one thing a test may not do.
oneDoorSurfaces.rawRuntimeNote: Ruling 14 — this holds BOTH spellings of the one act, the SDK import and the CLI spawn, because they are one target. Going around a door production has only one of is the one thing a test may not do, and a test spawning `claude` directly is doing exactly that.
oneDoorSurfaces.why: a test may cross any boundary to arrange the world; it may not go around a door production has only one of
oneDoorSurfaces.foreignTableWriteNote: Ruling 13. A test may write any foreign table directly — 63% of those writes would otherwise route through a function that is literally `insert(X).values(v)`. What is held is narrower and real: where the owner writes two rows in ONE call it has a cross-row invariant, and writing one without the other builds a state production cannot produce. The companion groups are derived from the owners' own writers, never listed.
